title: A JSON object with the same key twice parses fine - and silently keeps only the last one
assumption: A JSON parser rejects (or at least warns about) an object literal that repeats a key, the way a careful reviewer would.

input.description: A JSON payload assembled by string concatenation, a buggy serializer, or a merge of two partial objects that happens to repeat a key - e.g. a webhook payload built from two code paths that both set `"status"`.

what_goes_wrong: Both Python's `json.loads` and JavaScript's `JSON.parse` accept `{"a":1,"a":2}` without error and return `{"a": 2}` - the first value is discarded with no warning, exception, or trace that the input ever had a conflict.
why: The JSON grammar (RFC 8259 section 4) does not forbid duplicate names in an object: names SHOULD be unique, and when they aren't, the RFC says the behaviour of receiving software is unpredictable. The two languages then pin it down themselves. ECMA-262 specifies that `JSON.parse` overwrites a lexically earlier value with a later one for the same key, so last-wins is guaranteed in every conforming JavaScript engine. Python's `json` module documents the same choice: it does not raise and keeps only the last name/value pair. Other parsers in other languages may keep the first value or reject the document, which is how two services can read different values from the same payload.
fix: Detect duplicates explicitly where they matter. In Python, pass `object_pairs_hook` to `json.loads` and raise if a key repeats; in JavaScript, `JSON.parse` cannot report duplicates, so use a streaming/tokenizing parser that can, or reject them at the producer. Don't assume a successfully-parsed object had exactly the keys the sender wrote.

sources.title: RFC 8259: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format, Section 4
Python docs: json - JSON encoder and decoder

test_cases.note: their_parse(json_text) on an object with a repeated key returns the last value under standard parsers - if two upstream systems disagree about which value should win, catch this before trusting the parsed result.
